Babbitt woke at seven with the sound of the milk wagon rattling under his window, and for a minute he lay still, listening to the unremarkable noises of the street. Somewhere a dog barked. A neighbor’s furnace door clanged. He thought of the day ahead — the office, the lunch at the club, the dull little errands that made up a life — and felt, as he often did lately, a faint and unnamable dissatisfaction, as though he had mislaid something important in a drawer. His wife was already downstairs; he could hear the clink of dishes. He sat up, rubbed his face, and found his slippers with his feet. It was the same morning, he thought, as yesterday, and the one before that.
